To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
histone tails participate in the anchoring of the HIV-1 IN to the nucleosome for optimal integration into chromosomal DNA.
histone tails participate in the nucleosomal integration of HIV-1 by anchoring the viral intasome to chromatin.
histone tails participate in the anchoring of the HIV-1 integrative machinery to the chromatin, and that this anchoring is required for efficient integration and optimal viral replication.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of HIV-1 integration into chromatin and the role of histone tails in this process.
the molecular mechanism of HIV-1 integration into the host genome and how this process is modulated by the chromatin structure of the host cell.
the functional interactions between HIV-1 intesomes and nucleosomes, which play a key role in retroviral integration into host chromatin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amino-terminal tail is a major component in the nucleosome that interacts with HIV-1 IN, and that the IN/H4 interaction is important for the integration process.
the histone tails are not required for the intasome-nucleosome association, but they modulate this association and the efficiency of the integration process.
HIV-1 IN interacts with histone H4 tail in vitro and that this interaction is required for optimal integration of the viral DNA into chromatin in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
histone tails play a role in the nucleosomal integration of HIV-1.

histone tails participate in the functional association between IN and the nucleosome, which may have important consequences for the integration of the retrovirus into chromatin and its replication capacity.
histone tails may be involved in the anchoring of the HIV-1 integration complex (IN·viral DNA) to the nucleosome and thus in modulating the integration process in the host nucleus.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the amino-terminal tail from histone H4 can interact with the carboxy-terminus of HIV-1 IN to promote the functional association between IN and the nucleosome and to facilitate the insertion of the viral DNA genome into the host chromatin.

the intasome/nucleosome association is not a passive interaction but a dynamic process involving the amino-terminal tails of histones and the carboxy-terminus of IN that is important for integration and viral replication.
histone tails could be considered as a new class of host factors that modulate the HIV-1 integration process.
